summary:
Manisa falls squarely under Turkey's national legal and security framework. No statute, incident, police action or court decision specific to Manisa appears in the sources behind this record, so the assessment for a trans visitor is the national position as it applies in this province.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus '11th Judicial Package' would amend penal-code article 225 so that acts deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' carry up to three years' imprisonment, and same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to four years. The same package would amend civil-code article 40 ('Changing Sex') to raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25, add mandatory infertility conditions and government-approved hospital evaluation, and imprison care providers for up to seven years and trans patients for up to three. This is national legislation, not a provincial measure.

Three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025; none was submitted to parliament. A February 2026 press report described separate legislation considering criminalisation of public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years' imprisonment, which was not included in the 12th judicial package. The pattern in the reporting is that unpassed drafts have nonetheless shaped street-level enforcement: police stops of trans women for 'General Information Gathering' checks, and document demands at checkpoints, have proceeded while the prohibitions remained unenacted.

Carrying original photo identification is mandatory for foreign nationals at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. Every such interaction is an occasion on which a passport can be compared against presentation, which is the principal outing risk for a trans visitor in Manisa.

Pride events are banned in most years since 2015, with tear gas, water cannon and mass detentions used against those who defied the bans. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches; police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained, three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June and released on 8 August pending trial, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still running at year's end. ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow ranking placed Turkey 47th of 49.

In September 2026 coordinated raids under the 'My Family is Safe' crackdown involved 162 suspects, 9 associations and 13 businesses. Violence against trans people remains lethal: six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender people disproportionately affected.

Access to transition care is contracting. In June 2025 the health ministry's medicines agency banned prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21, despite existing law permitting access from 18. A visitor already on hormone therapy should expect questions at customs or at a pharmacy and should carry a prescription and a doctor's letter.
tangentialFactors:
Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and legal gender recognition has been available since 1988. The current pressure operates through draft penal legislation, administrative bans and policing practice rather than through a standing criminal prohibition on identity itself.

The gap between legislative status and enforcement is the recurring feature of the reporting. Three draft packages in 2025 were never submitted, and the February 2026 advocacy proposal was left out of the 12th judicial package, yet pride bans, association raids, 'General Information Gathering' stops and document checks continued throughout the same period. A visitor should read the unpassed status of a draft as no protection at street level.

Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, based on more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as evidence of the depth of the pattern rather than as a statement of current law.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners, no staff training to identify LGBT prisoners' needs, an administration operating on a binary basis, transfers that disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints mechanisms that are ineffective and can attract further violence. A trans prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025; rights groups demanded an independent investigation, reporting that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before, that medical staff arrived after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that placement follows registered sex.
localsOnly:
No comprehensive law in Turkey prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised. Marriage eligibility turns on the gender recorded in the civil registry, so a trans person who has legally changed the registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender.

Openly LGBTQ people are barred from the military. Legal gender recognition has been available since 1988, but one of the 2025 draft packages would have made it nearly impossible; that package was not submitted.

In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association for sharing 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values'. In September 2026 the 'My Family is Safe' crackdown produced coordinated raids involving 162 suspects, 9 associations and 13 businesses. National monitoring recorded a 2.5-fold rise in detentions during 2025, 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, family-year directives from the head of state, the closure of a rights organisation, and broadcast and arts-event censorship.

The Health Ministry's June 2025 medicines agency ban on hormones for under-21s applies to residents as well as visitors, and a September 2025 regulation following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular barred hospitals from recording the 'other' option on medical-board reports, requiring e-reports instead. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory records a Manisa-specific statute, prosecution, police action, hospital policy or court decision. Whether Manisa province has issued its own pride ban, its own 'My Family is Safe' operation, or its own health-directorate circular is unresolved on the available material.

The legislative status of the 11th Judicial Package is unresolved: Human Rights Watch reported it as a leaked draft before the government on 29 October 2025, and the inventory does not confirm whether it was subsequently enacted, amended or withdrawn. The same applies to the February 2026 proposal on public advocacy, which was reported as considered and then not included in the 12th judicial package.

The outcome of the 92 pride-related prosecutions reported as continuing at the end of 2025, and of the December 2025 dissolution order against the Young LGBTI+ Association, including any appeal, is not sourced here. Nor is the result of the demanded independent investigation into the 1 December 2025 death at Sincan Women's Prison.

Whether the June 2025 under-21 hormone ban has been challenged in court, and whether it is applied uniformly across Turkish hospitals including those in Manisa, is not established by these documents.
